discovery: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computation
motivation: Before 1995, many physicists believed decoherence made large-scale quantum computation impossible in principle: a continuous quantum state cannot be copied, and errors seemed fatal. Shor (1995) and Steane (1996) independently showed that redundantly encoding quantum information in entangled states of many physical systems allows errors to be detected and reversed without measuring, and so destroying, the encoded information. Shor then showed how to make computation fault-tolerant, and Kitaev introduced topological codes, notably the toric and surface codes, in which logical information lives in nonlocal degrees of freedom protected by locality. This led to the threshold theorem: below a finite physical error rate, logical errors can be suppressed exponentially. This is a deep physical statement about how quantum coherence can be preserved in a noisy macroscopic world. Recent experiments with superconducting, trapped-ion and neutral-atom processors have now shown logical qubits operating below threshold, so the idea has become a working technology.
